f: Content requires significant human involvement in the loop —AI can handle the writing, but a human editor must fact-check every piece because AI can pull wrong facts from the web, especially with outdated information or different model years. Without human strategy, topic selection, and verification, content becomes generic slop that looks identical to everyone else's.
The human-AI content partnership

Strategy and alignment must come first. Before any writing happens, dealerships need to understand which topics are actually useful to the end user —whether that's financing options, maintenance guides, inventory details, or local market insights. This topic selection is entirely a human decision.

AI can then generate the draft efficiently, but the real value emerges in the editing phase. A human editor familiar with the dealership's vehicles, market, and customers must verify every fact, especially dates, specifications, and pricing that change frequently across model years.
Why AI alone creates "slop"

When dealerships rely on AI without human oversight, all content starts to look like an even shade of gray —every dealer ends up with nearly identical answers pulled from the same web databases. This uniformity actually hurts visibility because AI search engines (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) have no reason to recommend one dealer over another when the content is interchangeable.

A Chevrolet dealer ranking first for "Silverado towing capacity" drives thousands of visits from researchers, not buyers ready to convert. Real dealership success means aligning content strategy to buyer intent and dealership profitability, not just search visibility.
The funnel mismatch problem

The core issue lies in distinguishing between research keywords and conversion keywords. A dealer can produce world-class content on technical specifications, features, or comparisons—the kind of material that ranks exceptionally well—but these high-funnel queries attract early-stage researchers , not immediate buyers. They read, learn, and leave without ever submitting a lead or visiting the dealership.

As Zach Billings explains in the Car Dealership Guy Podcast , the distinction between ranking and converting is fundamental to dealership strategy. A piece of content optimized for "best" searches near Fort Lauderdale, or inventory-specific queries, creates an entirely different outcome than broad educational content. The goal isn't visibility; the goal is outcomes tied to dealership profitability .
Why research traffic converts to zero sales

When a consumer searches for towing capacity, suspension details, or fuel economy comparisons, they are in research mode. They may visit multiple dealer websites, consume content from all of them, and still not be ready to purchase for weeks or months. Meanwhile, that traffic appears as a vanity metric in Google Analytics —impressive session numbers with no corresponding revenue.

962b1751bc.q: Why are repair orders declining in automotive dealerships?
962b1751bc.a: There are two competing explanations: Theory one, there are fewer units in operation coming through because of lower vehicle sales in prior year. Theory two, dealers are losing customers because we create too much friction, can't get someone on the phone, can't get an appointment, bad online scheduling, inaccurate wait times. Richard estimates UIO at 35-40 percent of the decline, with the remaining 60-65 percent attributable to dealer self-inflicted failure through friction in the customer experience.
962b1751bc.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live

ea49948c27.q: What role does customer friction play in repair order decline compared to market availability?
ea49948c27.a: Dave Rogers argues friction accounts for probably 50 percent of the issue, citing that dealers make it very difficult to do business through too many rules of engagement when customers call, poor phone availability, and an attitude of saying no first instead of yes. He emphasizes the need to say yes and find solutions like offering loaner vehicles rather than creating conditions that make customers hang up and go elsewhere.
ea49948c27.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
f: Customer friction accounts for roughly 50 percent of repair order decline , according to analysis presented at industry forums. Dealerships create this friction through restrictive rules of engagement, poor phone availability, and an instinctive reflex to say no instead of yes to customer requests—conditions that push customers toward competitors.
The friction factor: Why customers hang up

When customers call a dealership service department, they encounter multiple barriers designed to make the transaction difficult rather than easy. Too many rules of engagement force customers into narrow options, poor phone availability means long waits or unreturned calls, and an organizational culture of saying no first eliminates creative solutions that might retain the sale.

The contrast is stark: if a customer can easily reach a competing dealership, get answers quickly, and hear yes—perhaps in the form of a loaner vehicle or flexible appointment—they will choose that dealer. This is not a supply problem or a market problem; it's a business design problem. As discussed in the episode , the remedy is straightforward: reduce friction by making it easier, not harder, to do business.
When market availability is only half the story

The automotive industry has long blamed repair order decline on market factors—fewer vehicles in operation due to prior-year sales slumps, extended vehicle longevity, and supply chain constraints. These explanations account for only about 50 percent of the actual decline . The other half traces directly to self-inflicted friction that dealerships create.

be5e92f04e.q: How should dealership service departments answer incoming phone calls to improve customer retention?
be5e92f04e.a: Richard Lupo advocates for proactive solutions, noting that Apple Tree Automotive uses an AI agent that catches every single call, logs it, and schedules approximately 30 percent of appointments through AI with successful transfers. However, Tully Williams counters that he wants to maintain human-to-human contact during business hours, reserving AI for after-hours options, stating the dealership has been in business for 105 years and customers prefer talking to people rather than robots.
be5e92f04e.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
f: The debate hinges on a fundamental choice: AI agents that catch every call and schedule approximately 30 percent of appointments automatically , or maintaining human-to-human contact during business hours and reserving AI for after-hours overflow. There is no one-size-fits-all answer—both approaches have proven track records, and the best method depends on your dealership's customer expectations and operational capacity.

Richard Lupo advocates for a fully automated solution. His approach uses an AI agent that logs every incoming call and handles appointment scheduling without human intervention. This strategy eliminates missed calls—a real problem given that CDK data shows one in four service calls go on hold with an average hold time of 10 minutes. By automating the intake process, Lupo's system ensures no opportunity slips through the cracks.

Tully Williams represents the opposing view. He emphasizes that customer preference for human interaction remains strong , particularly during standard business hours. Williams operates a dealership with 105 years of history in his market, and his experience tells him that customers still value talking to a person rather than a robot. For his operation, the solution is hybrid: preserve the human touch when staff is available, and deploy AI only after hours when customers cannot reach a live representative.

Both leaders make a shared observation: customers have many service options available . As one panelist noted, "If customers have 16 other service options around them, our job is to become easier than those alternatives." This competitive pressure explains why both automation and accessibility matter, yet they frame solutions differently. Lupo's AI wins on speed and coverage; Williams's human-first approach wins on relationship and loyalty—a point discussed at length in the full panel discussion .

The practical implication is clear: your current call-handling failure rate matters more than the method . If you're losing calls to hold times or missed pickups, an AI agent with a 30 percent appointment conversion rate is likely better than a busy signal. If you're already answering most calls and your retention depends on relationship depth, the hybrid model—human during hours, AI after-hours—may preserve customer loyalty while still covering gaps.

For dealerships with smaller service teams or seasonal demand fluctuations, this episode explores in detail how both leaders implement their respective strategies and what metrics they track to measure success. The tension between automation and human touch is not resolved here—it's validated as a real operational choice that depends on your customer base and your ability to staff the phones consistently.

e3ab2fc33a.q: What percentage of routine vehicle service will migrate to mobile service outside dealership locations?
e3ab2fc33a.a: Ed Roberts predicted that within five years, 60 percent of service visits will be mobile. Richard Lupo estimates 50 percent of routine maintenance like oil changes and tire rotations will be done outside the brick-and-mortar facility within a few short years. Dave Rogers agrees that customers would accept this split, saying if dealers meet customers halfway on 50 percent of the work, customers will give them the other 50 percent.
e3ab2fc33a.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
f: Industry leaders predict that within five years, between 50 and 60 percent of routine vehicle maintenance will shift to mobile service outside dealership facilities. This transformation reflects a direct response to customer demand for convenience—dealers who meet customers halfway on this shift can retain the remaining service volume by remaining competitive.

The prediction comes from a consensus among fixed ops experts during a panel at the Chempress Supplier Summit. Ed Roberts forecasts 60 percent of service visits becoming mobile, while Richard Lupo estimates 50 percent of routine work like oil changes and tire rotations will move outside brick-and-mortar locations. The timeline is aggressive: both scenarios assume this shift occurs within just a few years.

This isn't speculation about remote diagnostics or theoretical convenience. As discussed in this panel conversation , mobile service is already operationally viable—Ed Roberts himself operates 40-some mobile vans handling 11,000 repair orders monthly, proving the model works at scale.
Why dealerships should accept the 50-50 split

Dave Rogers offers a pragmatic view: if dealers voluntarily embrace 50 percent mobile service, customers will reward them with the other 50 percent of their service business. The logic is straightforward—customers have 16 other service options in most markets, and they choose based on convenience and ease of doing business.

Resistance is understandable but shortsighted. Refusing mobile service doesn't prevent customers from using it elsewhere; it simply ensures they'll use it with a competitor. The panel explored how dealerships can become easier than those alternatives by meeting customers where they are, literally and operationally.

8e33c7f01f.q: Should dealerships prioritize gaining more customer demand or eliminating customer friction in service operations?
8e33c7f01f.a: Dave Rogers and Tully Williams both chose 20 percent more demand, with Tully noting he would turn increased demand into no friction anyway. Richard Lupo chose zero customer friction, arguing that if you create that experience, the business will build naturally. Sam Dark challenged Dave and Tully by asking why the market should give dealerships more customers if their current friction levels are leaking customers to the aftermarket.
8e33c7f01f.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
f: The panel split decisively: demand and friction are not equal priorities. Two leaders chose 20 percent more demand, betting they could convert it into frictionless operations , while one argued that eliminating friction first creates the foundation for organic growth. The tension reveals a fundamental truth: chasing new customers when your current experience drives them to competitors solves the wrong problem.

Dave Rogers and Tully Williams both voted for 20 percent more customer demand, with Tully noting he would immediately convert that increased volume into a seamless experience. Their logic assumes capacity and operational excellence can absorb new business—a reasonable bet for high-performing teams.

Richard Lupo took the opposite stance, choosing zero customer friction instead. His argument was direct: if you create a frictionless service experience, the business builds naturally . No marketing spend required. Customers stay. Referrals follow. Growth happens because you've earned it.

Sam Dark then posed a challenge that reframed the entire conversation. He asked Dave and Tully a sharper question: why should the market give dealerships more customers if current friction levels are already leaking existing customers to the aftermarket? The full debate on this strategic decision reveals how four of the industry's top fixed ops operators weigh growth against operational readiness.
"If customers have 16 other service options around them, our job is to become easier than those alternatives."

Panelist from Fixed Ops Friday — Captured during a debate on dealership service strategy at the Chempress Supplier Summit in Detroit, Michigan. The statement encapsulates the friction-first philosophy: in a saturated market, your only defensible advantage is ease of doing business.

397261cae0.q: How has OEM data sharing with parts suppliers impacted automotive parts availability in dealerships?
397261cae0.a: The panel discovered a significant supply chain problem: OEMs are not supplying their part suppliers with visibility into sales data, forcing suppliers to anticipate demand without that critical information. Dave Rogers found it fascinating that companies have extensive data but don't aggregate it for usefulness, leaving suppliers unable to know parts availability. Tully Williams noted that parts suppliers are asking OEMs to simply give them the data so they can better anticipate part needs.
397261cae0.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
f: OEMs possess extensive sales data but don't aggregate or share it with parts suppliers, forcing suppliers to anticipate demand without visibility into actual market needs. This blind spot leaves dealership shelves vulnerable to parts shortages, even when the data exists to prevent them.

The supply chain problem emerged during a panel discussion at the Chempress Supplier Summit in Detroit, Michigan. Panel members discovered that companies across the automotive industry have access to granular sales information—vehicle models sold, service intervals followed, replacement patterns—yet this data remains siloed internally rather than shared downstream with the parts suppliers who must stock inventory.

Parts suppliers are explicitly asking OEMs to simply provide access to this sales data. As discussed during the panel , the barrier is not technical—OEMs can extract and share this information—but organizational. Suppliers lack the demand signals needed to make informed purchasing decisions, so they resort to guessing which parts will be needed and in what volumes.

The consequence ripples through dealership service departments. When suppliers can't predict demand accurately, they either stock too conservatively and parts become unavailable, or they overstock and capital ties up in slow-moving inventory. The conversation at Chempress revealed this was not a problem anyone on the panel had anticipated before the summit, suggesting it's widespread across the industry but largely unexamined.

What makes this pattern especially notable is that the data already exists within OEM systems . The solution doesn't require new technology or costly infrastructure—it requires a shift in how OEMs think about data sharing as a competitive advantage for the entire supply chain, not a proprietary asset to be guarded.
Data Visibility as the Missing Link

9beb669963.q: Should dealerships follow OEM-recommended maintenance intervals or adopt more frequent service schedules?
9beb669963.a: Tully Williams was the sole dissenter on the panel, believing the factory should dictate maintenance intervals and dealerships should stay by those factory standards. The other three guests advocated for more advanced rotation schedules, such as oil changes every six months, whereas Tully's manufacturers predominantly recommend one-year intervals. Tully emphasized the importance of adhering to factory standards set by OEM engineers.
9beb669963.e: Fixed Ops Friday w/ Dave Rogers, Tully Williams, Ed Roberts, & Richard Lupo | Daily Dealer Live
f: There is genuine disagreement among dealership leaders on this question. While Tully Williams advocated for strictly adhering to OEM-recommended maintenance intervals —typically one-year intervals set by factory engineers—three other panelists pushed for more aggressive schedules, including oil changes every six months, to better align with how customers actually use their vehicles.
The Factory Standard Argument

Tully Williams took a firm position: manufacturers engineer their maintenance intervals based on extensive testing and real-world data, and dealerships should respect that expertise rather than second-guess it. OEM engineers deliberately set intervals to balance durability, cost, and customer value , and deviating from those standards risks undermining the integrity of the vehicle warranty and the automaker's research.

This perspective treats the factory standard as a baseline of trust—if a manufacturer says a vehicle's oil is good for 12 months, overriding that decision without explicit customer agreement could expose the dealership to liability and damage relationships with the OEM supply chain.
The Advanced Service Schedule Perspective

The three other panelists took a different view: customers do not always drive their vehicles in the conditions OEMs assume when they design maintenance schedules. Stop-and-go city driving, towing, or extreme temperatures can degrade fluid faster than a manufacturer's one-year projection.

a1046603b1.q: What soft skills should car dealership managers prioritize in training their sales teams to gain competitive advantage?
a1046603b1.a: David Zuniga emphasizes that soft skills—mindset, attitude, grit, and persistence—are the real difference in developing salespeople, not just product and process training. He stresses the importance of mental preparation, noting that preparation builds confidence, which customers can relate to and seek when buying.
a1046603b1.e: Zuniga on People, Novoa on Co-op, Kline on Risk | Daily Dealer Live
f: Soft skills— mindset, attitude, grit, and persistence —are the real difference in developing salespeople, not product and process training alone. Preparation builds confidence, and customers recognize and respond to that confidence when buying.

The traditional focus on product knowledge and sales process falls short if salespeople lack the foundational mental approach to succeed. As discussed in the Car Dealership Guy Podcast , the moment a salesperson enters the dealership floor, their internal state—their willingness to close a deal, their resilience in handling rejection, their hunger to perform—directly influences how customers perceive and trust them.

Mental preparation is the foundation of this confidence. When salespeople invest time in preparing their mindset each day, they walk the floor with clarity and conviction. This isn't abstract psychology; it's visible to the customer immediately. A prepared salesperson carries themselves differently, asks better questions, and closes more deals because their attitude attracts rather than resists.
Grit and persistence as a training priority

Among the nine salespeople at Performance Auto Group's Kia dealership in Denville, New Jersey, the difference between top performers and struggling ones rarely comes down to how well they memorize trim levels or payment calculations. It comes down to how they bounce back from rejection and whether they view obstacles as temporary setbacks or permanent defeats.

Training programs that focus only on scripts and closing techniques miss the psychological dimension entirely. Managers who invest in building grit—teaching salespeople to persist through slow months, handle objections without taking them personally, and maintain energy in competitive markets—create a team that survives downturns and thrives in growth.

e176179a66.q: How can dealership salespeople improve their performance by preparing mentally before customer interactions?
e176179a66.a: Zuniga explains that what happens between opportunities is critical. Preparation builds confidence, and confidence is what customers are looking for. He uses sports analogies, noting that football players prepare mentally before a game, yet sales professionals often jump into interactions without that mental preparation.
e176179a66.e: Zuniga on People, Novoa on Co-op, Kline on Risk | Daily Dealer Live
f: What happens between opportunities is critical—preparation builds the confidence that customers are actually looking for . Most sales professionals jump into customer interactions without mental preparation, even though athletes across all sports spend significant time preparing mentally before competition.

David Zuniga draws a direct parallel to how football players mentally prepare before a game. They visualize plays, review strategy, and align themselves mentally—yet in car sales, many representatives skip this essential step entirely. The moment a customer walks onto the lot, that salesperson must already be mentally ready.

This preparation isn't complicated, but it is deliberate. As Zuniga explains in the episode , the first person a salesperson has to close every day is themselves. Self-closure—mental alignment and intention-setting—directly determines how they show up with customers.
"Every day the first person we have to close is ourselves. What did we come here to do today?"

David Zuniga — General Sales Manager, Performance Auto Group. Zuniga has spent over 15 years in the automotive industry, rising through BDC, sales desk, and closing roles before taking on management. He now leads nine salespeople at Performance Auto Group's Kia dealership in Denville, New Jersey, and oversees an in-house BDC operation. His approach to sales development centers on mindset and mental readiness as the foundation of sustainable performance.

The logic is straightforward: customer confidence mirrors salesperson confidence. If a salesperson arrives at the customer interaction already mentally prepared—clear on the day's goals, emotionally centered, and intentional—that state transmits to the customer. It's not about manipulation; it's about showing up as a grounded, focused professional rather than reactive and scattered.

468bbd8088.q: What is the toughest position to hire for in automotive dealerships in 2026?
468bbd8088.a: According to Zuniga, sales professionals are the toughest role to hire for because the industry is stuck in approaches that used to work, while today's new salespeople need a different coaching style, development approach, and training methodology. Dealerships must adjust their styles to set new hires up to win.
468bbd8088.e: Zuniga on People, Novoa on Co-op, Kline on Risk | Daily Dealer Live
f: Sales professionals are the hardest role to fill because dealerships remain locked in outdated coaching and training methods that no longer work for today's salespeople . The industry continues applying approaches that succeeded in the past, but new hires need fundamentally different development strategies to thrive.

The core challenge isn't finding candidates—it's adapting the organization itself. As David Zuniga explains in the episode , dealerships must fundamentally shift how they coach, develop, and train incoming sales talent .

The mismatch occurs because veteran managers often default to the methods that got them to their current position. What worked for them in an earlier era of dealership sales simply doesn't resonate with new hires entering an industry that has transformed. This generational gap in training philosophy is at the heart of the sales hiring crisis .
Adjusting Your Approach to Set New Hires Up to Win

Zuniga, who manages nine salespeople at Performance Auto Group's Kia dealership in Denville, New Jersey, emphasizes that dealers must actively redesign their coaching style to match how new salespeople learn and perform best. The old playbook no longer guarantees success.

This isn't about lowering standards or abandoning proven sales fundamentals. Rather, it's about recognizing that the delivery mechanism, the motivation triggers, and the feedback loop all need to evolve with the workforce . Dealerships that continue forcing yesterday's training model onto today's recruits inevitably watch them leave for competitors or industries where their development feels more relevant.

100c7a828a.q: What qualities should automotive managers possess to effectively develop and retain salespeople?
100c7a828a.a: Zuniga states that managers must like people, want to develop them, and have fulfillment from building people up rather than tearing them down. The best managers have patience, time, and energy to see someone who isn't a finished product and commit to developing them into a success.

f: Automotive managers must genuinely like people and want to develop them , finding fulfillment in building salespeople up rather than tearing them down. The best managers invest patience, time, and energy to see potential in people who aren't yet finished products, and commit to developing them into success.
The Foundation: People-First Leadership

The difference between a manager who develops talent and one who doesn't starts with a fundamental mindset. David Zuniga, who manages nine salespeople at Performance Auto Group's Kia dealership in Denville, New Jersey, emphasizes that genuine care for people is non-negotiable . A manager's primary focus must be on the human being in front of them, not merely on hitting numbers or meeting quotas.

This people-centered approach requires a specific emotional posture: managers must find real satisfaction in helping others grow. As Zuniga explains in the episode , the alternative—finding fulfillment in criticism or control—actively destroys team capability and turns over salespeople at a costly rate.
The Investment: Patience, Time, and Energy

Great managers understand that developing people takes sustained resources . A salesperson starting out or struggling in their role is not a finished failure; they're a work in progress that demands deliberate attention. Zuniga's approach with his team reflects this: he doesn't expect immediate mastery, but rather commits to the gradual process of skill-building and confidence growth.

b8a99c962d.q: What is the biggest obstacle to maintaining sales momentum and growth in a dealership?
b8a99c962d.a: Zuniga identifies continuing the momentum already built as the primary obstacle, not just maintaining current numbers but graduating into new problems and higher standards. He emphasizes that teams should always be developing and growing into new challenges rather than going backwards.
